cues.text: Around 1399, in the marshy meadows outside the Polish city of Poznan, a consecrated Host was discovered under circumstances that drew an immediate and lasting popular devotion.
A Eucharistic following developed almost at once, and within a year, in 1400, a papal bull recognized the devotion forming there.

By the following century, a fuller and considerably more dramatic account had taken hold in popular memory: a servant girl, bribed by men hostile to the faith, had stolen three consecrated Hosts from a Dominican church.
The men pierced the Hosts with sharp instruments in a nearby house, causing them to bleed.
Attempting to dispose of the evidence in the same marsh, they saw the Hosts rise into the air surrounded by light before the local bishop was able to recover them.
This account — vivid, and repeated in countless devotional retellings since — is the version most commonly told of the Poznan miracle today.
The Archdiocese of Poznan itself, examining its own medieval sources, states plainly that the desecration-and-bleeding narrative cannot be documented in contemporary records.
It states that the confirmed historical core is considerably more modest: a Host found in the meadow, and the intense, well-attested popular devotion that followed.
The more elaborate story of theft and profanation appears to be a later embellishment layered onto a genuine, if simpler, original devotion.
A Church Built on the Site
In 1406, King Wladyslaw Jagiello, having made his own pilgrimage to venerate the Host, granted land for a new church to be built directly on the site of the marsh, dedicated to the Body of Christ.

Construction proved difficult given the wet ground, but by the following century the resulting Corpus Christi Church had become one of the most important Eucharistic shrines in all of Poland, a standing it has held for over six hundred years.
The Hosts venerated at Corpus Christi Church in Poznan continue to draw a weekly Eucharistic procession every Thursday, six centuries after events on the site first drew pilgrims.

Whatever the precise shape of the original fourteenth-century happening — a straightforward, well-attested discovery, later dressed in a more elaborate story of theft and desecration — the underlying devotion it produced has endured.
It has proven durable enough to stand the test of time.
